chapters.n: Paul opens forcefully: his apostleship came neither from any human source nor through human appointment, but from Jesus Christ and the Father who raised Him. Critics in Galatia had questioned his authority.

f.w: not of men, neither by man

chapters.n: He writes with the brethren traveling with him to the congregations of Galatia, a region in central Asia Minor (modern Turkey).

f.g: Likely the congregations Paul founded in towns like Antioch of Pisidia, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe.

chapters.n: His usual blessing of grace and peace from the Father and the Son.

f.w: Grace be to you and peace

chapters.n: Christ gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age, as the Father willed. The Atonement is front and center from the first lines.

f.g: This present wicked age.

chapters.n: To God be glory forever.

f.g: Literally “to the ages of the ages.”

chapters.n: Skipping his usual thanksgiving, Paul expresses shock that they are so quickly turning from God, who called them by Christ’s grace, to a different “gospel.”

f.g: Quickly deserting — like a soldier defecting.

chapters.n: There really is no other gospel. Some people are troubling them, trying to distort the gospel of Christ — teachers who insisted Gentile converts be circumcised and keep the law of Moses.

f.g: Twist, distort.

chapters.n: Even if Paul or an angel from heaven preached a different gospel, let that one be accursed. The message matters more than the messenger.

f.g: Greek anathema — under God’s curse.

chapters.n: He repeats it for emphasis: anyone preaching another gospel than the one they received stands under God’s curse.

f.g: He had warned them during his visits.

chapters.n: Is Paul trying to win human approval or God’s? If he were still pleasing people, he couldn’t be Christ’s servant.

f.w: do I seek to please men?

chapters.n: He assures them the gospel he preached did not originate with any human.

f.g: Not of human origin.

chapters.n: He didn’t receive it or learn it from people, but by revelation from Jesus Christ.

f.w: by the revelation of Jesus Christ

chapters.n: They know his past: as a zealous Jew he violently persecuted God’s Church and tried to destroy it.

f.g: Conduct, way of life.
Ravaged, laid waste.

chapters.n: He outpaced many his age in Judaism, being extremely zealous for the traditions of his ancestors.

f.g: The oral traditions of the Pharisees.

chapters.n: But God set Paul apart even before birth and called him by grace — echoing Jeremiah’s call.

f.w: separated me from my mother's womb

chapters.n: God revealed His Son to Paul so he could preach Christ to the Gentiles. Paul didn’t immediately consult anyone.

f.g: The Gentiles, non-Jewish nations.
Human beings.

chapters.n: He didn’t go to the earlier apostles in Jerusalem; he went into Arabia and then returned to Damascus.

f.g: Probably the Nabataean kingdom east and south of Damascus.

chapters.n: Three years later he went to Jerusalem to get acquainted with Peter, staying fifteen days.

f.g: Greek historeo — to visit to get to know or inquire.

chapters.n: The only other apostle he met then was James, the Lord’s brother.
Before God, Paul declares he is not lying — showing how seriously his independence was being challenged.
Next he went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia, including his hometown, Tarsus.

f.g: A region in southeast Asia Minor; Tarsus was its chief city.

chapters.n: The congregations in Judea didn’t know him personally.

f.g: Not personally acquainted.

chapters.n: They only heard that their former persecutor now preached the faith he once tried to destroy.
And they praised God because of the change in Paul. A transformed life is a powerful witness.
Fourteen years later Paul returned to Jerusalem with Barnabas and Titus, a Gentile convert. Many link this with the Jerusalem council in Acts 15.
He went by revelation and privately laid out his gospel before the leading apostles, to be sure his work among Gentiles was in harmony with theirs.

f.g: In response to divine direction.
The recognized leaders of the Church.

chapters.n: Yet the leaders didn’t require Titus, a Greek, to be circumcised — a test case proving Gentiles needn’t live the law of Moses.
The issue arose because false believers had slipped in to spy on the freedom believers have in Christ, hoping to enslave them under the law.

f.g: Secretly.

chapters.n: Paul didn’t yield to them for a moment, so the true gospel would be preserved for the Galatians.

f.g: Gave in, submitted.

chapters.n: The respected leaders — whatever their standing, which God doesn’t weigh — added nothing to Paul’s message.
Instead they recognized that Paul had been entrusted with the gospel to the Gentiles, as Peter had been to the Jews.

f.g: The mission to the Gentiles.

chapters.n: The same God who worked through Peter among Jews worked powerfully through Paul among Gentiles.

f.g: Worked powerfully.

chapters.n: James, Peter, and John, the pillars of the Church, recognized God’s grace in Paul and shook hands with him and Barnabas in fellowship, dividing their missionary focus.

f.g: Main supports — key leaders of the Church.
A handshake signaling formal agreement and partnership.

chapters.n: Their only request was that Paul remember the poor — something he was eager to do.
Later, when Peter came to Antioch, Paul confronted him to his face because Peter was clearly in the wrong.

f.g: Antioch in Syria, an early center of Gentile Christianity.

chapters.n: Peter had been eating with Gentile believers, but when men came from James, he pulled back, afraid of the circumcision party.

f.w: he did eat with the Gentiles
them which were of the circumcision
f.g: Jewish Christians who insisted on the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Other Jewish believers joined in this hypocrisy, and even Barnabas was swept along.

f.g: Pretended, acted hypocritically.

chapters.n: Paul publicly asked Peter: if you, a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you force Gentiles to live like Jews? Even an apostle could be corrected about how a principle was applied.

f.g: Weren’t walking straight in line with the gospel.

chapters.n: Paul continues: we were born Jews, not Gentile “sinners” as Jews then labeled outsiders.

f.g: A common Jewish label for those outside the covenant law.

chapters.n: Yet even Jews know a person is put right with God not by keeping the law’s works but through faith in Jesus Christ. No one is justified by the law.

f.w: not justified by the works of the law

f.g: Declared righteous; brought into right relationship with God.

chapters.n: If seeking justification in Christ shows we are sinners (by the law’s standard), does that make Christ promote sin? Absolutely not!

f.g: A servant or promoter of sin.
Certainly not!

chapters.n: If Paul rebuilt the system of law he had torn down, he would prove himself a lawbreaker.

f.w: build again the things which I destroyed
f.g: Restore the law as a way to be justified.

chapters.n: Through the law he died to the law, so he could live for God. The law itself pointed him to Christ.
Paul’s old self was crucified with Christ. Now Christ lives in him, and his mortal life is lived by faith in the Son of God, who loved him and gave Himself for him.

f.w: who loved me, and gave himself for me

chapters.n: Paul won’t set aside God’s grace. If righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing.

f.g: Nullify, set aside.

chapters.n: “You foolish Galatians! Who has put a spell on you?” Christ’s crucifixion had been preached to them so vividly it was like a poster displayed before their eyes.

f.g: Cast a spell on, like the evil eye.
Publicly placarded, displayed like a notice.

chapters.n: One question: did they receive the Holy Ghost by keeping the law, or by hearing and believing?

f.g: Hearing the message with faith.

chapters.n: Having started by the Spirit, do they now think they can finish by human effort?

f.g: Completed by outward rituals like circumcision.

chapters.n: Did they suffer so much for nothing? Surely it wasn’t for nothing.

f.g: Possibly persecution, or simply “experienced so much.”

chapters.n: Does God give them the Spirit and work miracles among them because they keep the law, or because they believe?
It’s like Abraham: he believed God, and God counted it as righteousness.
So people of faith are Abraham’s true children.

Scripture foresaw God justifying Gentiles by faith and announced the gospel to Abraham in advance: “In you all nations shall be blessed.” Latter-day scripture confirms the gospel was taught to Abraham.

f.w: In thee shall all nations be blessed
preached before the gospel unto Abraham

chapters.n: So those who have faith share in faithful Abraham’s blessing.
Those relying on the law are under its curse, because the law curses anyone who fails to do everything it requires — and no one manages that.

f.w: Cursed is every one that continueth not

chapters.n: Clearly no one is made right with God by the law, since Habakkuk says the righteous will live by faith.

f.w: The just shall live by faith

chapters.n: The law works on a different principle: whoever does its commands will live by them.

f.w: The man that doeth them shall live in them

chapters.n: Christ freed us from the law’s curse by taking the curse on Himself. The law said anyone hung on a tree was cursed — and Jesus was hung on a cross.

f.w: Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree

f.g: Bought back, freed by paying a price.

chapters.n: So Abraham’s blessing could reach Gentiles through Christ, and we could receive the promised Spirit through faith.
An everyday example: once a human agreement is ratified, no one can cancel it or add terms.

f.g: Greek diatheke — a covenant or will/testament.
Cancels, annuls.

chapters.n: God’s promises were given to Abraham and his “seed” (offspring). Paul notes the singular word and applies it ultimately to Christ.
The law of Moses, coming 430 years later, can’t cancel the covenant God earlier ratified with Abraham.
If the inheritance depended on the law, it wouldn’t come by promise — but God gave it to Abraham freely as a promise.
Why the law, then? It was added because of transgressions, until Christ came, and was given through angels by a mediator — Moses. The JST expands these verses to clarify Moses’ role.

f.w: It was added because of transgressions

f.g: A go-between — here, Moses.

chapters.n: A mediator implies two parties, but God is one. Many scholars call this one of Paul’s most puzzling verses. The JST adds that Christ is the one mediator of the new covenant.

f.w: a mediator is not a mediator of one

chapters.n: Is the law opposed to God’s promises? Certainly not! But no law could give life; otherwise righteousness would have come that way.

f.w: a law given which could have given life

chapters.n: Scripture shows everyone is trapped under sin, so the promise could be given through faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe.

f.g: Locked up everyone under sin.

chapters.n: Before faith in Christ came, we were held in custody under the law, kept for the faith that would be revealed.

f.g: Confined, guarded.

chapters.n: The law was our tutor or guardian, bringing us to Christ so we could be justified by faith.

f.g: Greek paidagogos — a trusted slave who supervised and escorted a child to school, not the teacher himself.

chapters.n: Now that faith has come, we no longer need that guardian.
All of them are God’s children through faith in Christ Jesus.
All who were baptized into Christ have “put on” Christ, like putting on new clothing that identifies them as His.
In Christ, divisions of ethnicity, social class, and gender vanish in terms of worth and access to salvation — all are one.
And if they belong to Christ, they are Abraham’s offspring and heirs of God’s promises.
Paul compares God’s people before Christ to an underage heir: though he will own everything, while a child he has no more freedom than a servant.

f.g: In Roman law a minor heir was under guardians until a set age.

chapters.n: He is under guardians and managers until the date his father has set.

f.g: Guardians and estate managers.

chapters.n: Likewise, before Christ, we were like children enslaved to the basic principles of this world.

f.g: Basic principles or elementary rules — possibly also spiritual forces.

chapters.n: But at exactly the right time, God sent His Son, born of a woman and born under the law — fully human, fully subject to the law.
He came to redeem those under the law, so we could be adopted as God’s sons and daughters with full rights.
Because they are His children, God sent the Spirit of His Son into their hearts, crying, “Abba, Father!” — an intimate Aramaic word for father.

f.g: Aramaic for “father,” used by children in close, loving address.

chapters.n: So you are no longer a slave but a child — and if a child, then an heir of God through Christ.
Before knowing God, these Gentiles served beings that are not truly gods.
Now that they know God — or rather are known by Him — why go back to weak, worthless principles and be enslaved again?

f.g: Poor, powerless rules.

chapters.n: They were carefully observing special days, months, seasons, and years — perhaps Jewish festival calendars imposed as requirements for salvation.

f.w: days, and months, and times, and years

chapters.n: Paul fears his work among them may have been wasted.
He pleads: become free like me, because I became like you Gentiles. You didn’t wrong me before.

f.g: Free from the law as a means of justification.

chapters.n: They remember that it was because of an illness that Paul first preached to them.

f.g: A physical illness, possibly connected to his “thorn in the flesh.”

chapters.n: Though his condition was a trial to them, they didn’t despise him but welcomed him as an angel — even as Christ Jesus.

f.w: my temptation which was in my flesh
f.g: His physical condition, which tested them.

chapters.n: What happened to their joy? They would have torn out their own eyes for him — which some take as a hint that Paul’s illness affected his eyes.

f.g: Possibly a hint of an eye problem; or simply an expression of devotion.

chapters.n: Has he become their enemy for telling them the truth?

f.w: because I tell you the truth

chapters.n: The false teachers court them eagerly, but not for good. They want to shut them out from Paul so they’ll be devoted to them instead.

f.g: Eagerly court your favor.

chapters.n: It is good to be eagerly sought for good purposes, at all times — not just while Paul is present.

f.g: For a good purpose.

chapters.n: Paul feels like a mother in labor again for them, until Christ is fully formed in them.

f.g: Suffer labor pains.

f.w: until Christ be formed in you

chapters.n: He wishes he could be with them to speak in a gentler tone, because he is perplexed about them.

f.g: Speak in a different tone.

chapters.n: To those wanting to be under the law: do you actually listen to what the law (the books of Moses) says?

f.g: Here, the Torah — the five books of Moses.

chapters.n: Genesis says Abraham had two sons: Ishmael by Hagar, a servant woman, and Isaac by Sarah, a free woman.

f.g: Slave woman.

chapters.n: Ishmael was born in the ordinary way; Isaac was born because of God’s promise.
Paul treats this as an allegory of two covenants. Hagar represents the covenant from Mount Sinai, whose children are born into bondage.

f.g: A story used to illustrate a spiritual truth.
Greek form of Hagar.

chapters.n: Hagar stands for Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the earthly Jerusalem of Paul’s day, in bondage with her children under the law.

f.g: Corresponds to.

chapters.n: But the heavenly Jerusalem is free, and she is our mother.
Paul quotes Isaiah: the barren woman will rejoice, for she will have more children than the married one — a promise of a vast family through grace.
Believers, like Isaac, are children of promise.
As Ishmael mocked Isaac, so now those born of the flesh persecute those born of the Spirit.
Scripture says: “Cast out the slave woman and her son,” for he won’t share the inheritance with the free woman’s son.

f.w: Cast out the bondwoman and her son

chapters.n: So believers are children not of slavery but of freedom.
Christ has set us free. So stand firm and don’t let yourselves be harnessed again to a yoke of slavery.

f.w: the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free

chapters.n: If they accept circumcision as necessary for salvation, Christ will be of no benefit to them.

f.g: Adopting circumcision as a requirement for salvation.

chapters.n: Anyone who accepts circumcision on that basis is obligated to keep the entire law of Moses.

f.w: a debtor to do the whole law

chapters.n: Those trying to be justified by the law have cut themselves off from Christ and fallen away from grace.
But through the Spirit, by faith, believers eagerly await the righteousness they hope for.
In Christ, circumcision or lack of it means nothing. What counts is faith that expresses itself through love.
They were running the race well. Who cut in and tripped them up from obeying the truth?

f.g: Literally “cut in on” — like a runner blocked on the track.

chapters.n: This persuasion doesn’t come from God, who called them.

f.g: This new teaching.

chapters.n: A little yeast works through the whole batch of dough — a little false teaching can corrupt the whole community.

f.w: A little leaven leaveneth the whole lump

chapters.n: Paul is confident in the Lord they’ll agree with him. Whoever is troubling them will bear God’s judgment.
If Paul still preached circumcision, as some claimed, why is he persecuted? Preaching circumcision would remove the offense of the cross.
With biting sarcasm, Paul wishes those so eager for cutting would cut themselves off completely.

f.g: A sharp play on words about circumcision; possibly “mutilate themselves.”

chapters.n: They were called to freedom — but not as an excuse to indulge selfish desires. Instead, serve one another in love.

f.g: An opportunity for the sinful nature.

chapters.n: The whole law is summed up in one command: love your neighbor as yourself.

f.w: Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself

chapters.n: If they bite and devour each other like wild animals, they’ll end up destroying one another.

f.g: Picture of animals fighting.

chapters.n: Live by the Spirit, and you won’t carry out the desires of the sinful nature.

f.g: Desires of the fallen, natural self.

chapters.n: The flesh and the Spirit are at war with each other, pulling in opposite directions.

f.w: the flesh lusteth against the Spirit

chapters.n: Those led by the Spirit are not under the law’s condemnation.
The works of the sinful nature are obvious: sexual sin, impurity, and shameless sensuality.

f.g: Shameless indecency.
Moral impurity.

chapters.n: Idolatry, sorcery, hostility, conflict, jealousy, rage, rivalry, divisions, and factions.

f.g: Greek pharmakeia — sorcery, often involving drugs.
Jealous rivalries.
Dissensions and factions.

chapters.n: Envy, murder, drunkenness, wild partying, and the like. Paul warns again: those who live this way won’t inherit God’s kingdom.

f.g: Drunken carousing.

f.w: shall not inherit the kingdom of God

chapters.n: But the fruit the Spirit grows in us is love, joy, peace, patience, gentleness, goodness, and faithfulness. Note it is one “fruit” — a single harvest of Christlike character.

f.g: Patience.

chapters.n: Meekness and self-control. No law forbids such things.

f.g: Self-control.

chapters.n: Those who belong to Christ have crucified the sinful nature with its passions and desires.
Since the Spirit gives us life, let us keep in step with the Spirit.

f.g: Keep in step, march in line.

chapters.n: Let’s not be conceited, provoking and envying each other.

f.g: Empty pride, conceit.

chapters.n: If someone is caught in a sin, spiritually mature members should gently help restore him — keeping watch over themselves so they aren’t tempted too.

f.g: Greek katartizo — to mend, like setting a broken bone or repairing a net.

chapters.n: Carry each other’s burdens, and so fulfill Christ’s law of love.
Anyone who thinks he is something special when he is nothing is fooling himself.
Each should examine his own work. Then he can take satisfaction in it without comparing himself to others.

f.g: Test, examine his own conduct.

chapters.n: Each person must carry his own load of responsibility before God.

f.g: A different word from verse 2 — a personal pack every soldier carries.

chapters.n: Those taught the gospel should share good things with their teachers.

f.g: Share, give a portion.

chapters.n: Don’t be fooled: God can’t be mocked. People reap what they sow.

f.w: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap

chapters.n: Sow to selfish desires and you reap decay; sow to the Spirit and you reap eternal life.
Don’t get tired of doing good. At the right time we will reap a harvest if we don’t give up.

f.w: let us not be weary in well doing

chapters.n: Whenever we have the opportunity, do good to everyone — especially fellow members of the household of faith.

f.g: Fellow believers, the Church family.

chapters.n: Paul takes the pen himself: see what large letters he uses as he writes in his own hand — perhaps for emphasis, or because of poor eyesight.

f.g: Literally “with what large letters.”

chapters.n: Those pushing circumcision want to look good outwardly and avoid persecution for preaching the cross of Christ.

f.w: a fair shew in the flesh
f.g: A good outward impression.

chapters.n: Even they don’t keep the whole law. They want the Galatians circumcised so they can boast about it.

f.g: Boast of your circumcision as a trophy.

chapters.n: Paul will boast only in the cross of Christ. Through it, the world is dead to him and he is dead to the world.

f.w: the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ
the world is crucified unto me

chapters.n: In Christ, being circumcised or not means nothing; what matters is becoming a new creation.
Peace and mercy on all who follow this rule — the true Israel of God, defined by faith in Christ.

f.g: God’s covenant people, Jew and Gentile united in Christ.

chapters.n: From now on, let no one trouble Paul, because he bears the scars of Jesus on his body — the marks of beatings and stoning endured for Christ.

f.w: the marks of the Lord Jesus
f.g: Greek stigmata — brand marks; here, his scars of persecution.

chapters.n: Paul closes with a blessing of Christ’s grace on their spirits, addressing them warmly as brothers and sisters.

f.w: the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ
